notes: Lesson Overview (10 min): Welcome students to Class 2. Frame today around 5 core milestones: Object Identification, Collections, Timers, Events, Google Play. Emphasize that Basics 2 moves beyond simple scripts into architectural communication.

title: Course Roadmap & 5 Milestones
content:
5 Core Architecture Milestones
1. Who Did We Hit?

Detect enemies cleanly with CompareTag and TryGetComponent without frame drops.

2. The Data Locker

Choose between Arrays (fixed), Lists (expanding), and ScriptableObjects (shared brain).

3. Timing & Coroutines

Build weapon cooldowns and spawner routines with yield return new WaitForSeconds().

4. Broadcaster Events

Radio station pattern: fire events to UI and audio systems with zero spaghetti coupling.

5. Google Play Pipeline

Sign keystores, build Android App Bundles (.aab), and prepare for mobile release.

[Advanced] Architecture Rule: When Should Scripts Talk? Expand ▼
1. Exclusive 1-to-1 relationship? Direct reference ([SerializeField] private Weapon weapon;). 2. One trigger affects multiple systems? C# Event (public static event Action OnPlayerDied;). 3. Shared game data? ScriptableObject ([CreateAssetMenu]).
[Expert] Fast Iteration with Assembly Definitions Expand ▼
Split scripts into Core.asmdef, Enemies.asmdef, and UI.asmdef. Saves 80% recompilation time on large projects!
notes: Roadmap (5 min): Walk through the 5 milestones. Ask students: 'How many of you had scripts that broke when an object was renamed?' Preview that today solves that.

title: 1. GameObject Identification
subtitle: Recognizing, Filtering & Targeting Collided GameObjects in 2D Space
content:
The Core Challenge
Physics collisions inform us that two colliders touched. Our code must immediately determine what kind of entity was struck and execute the corresponding gameplay logic cleanly.
notes: Part 1: Identification (2 min): Transition slide. Explain that collisions in 2D give us basic physical contact, but gameplay requires knowing *what* we hit.

title: Collisions: What Did We Just Hit?
content:
OnCollisionEnter2D & Stomp Detection

Runs once when two solid physical colliders bump into each other:

void OnCollisionEnter2D(Collision2D other) {
    // Check if player landed on top of the enemy
    Vector2 normal = other.GetContact(0).normal;
    if (normal.y > 0.5f) {
        SquashEnemy();
    } else {
        TakeDamage(10);
    }
}
Contact Normal Math: other.GetContact(0).normal is a directional vector pointing outward from the impact surface. If normal.y > 0.5f, the collision came from above (stomp). If normal.y is near 0.0f, it was a horizontal side impact.
The Golden Collision Rule
Both objects need a Collider2D, and at least ONE needs a Rigidbody2D!
If neither object has a Rigidbody2D, Unity's 2D physics engine does not calculate physical collisions, and OnCollisionEnter2D will never fire. For static platforms, leave Rigidbody off; for characters, always add Rigidbody2D.
[LIVE PHYSICS SIMULATOR: Collision Normal]
normal (0, 1)
Click an action above to simulate collision normal math.
[Advanced] Contact Points Memory Expand ▼
Using other.GetContact(0) avoids memory allocation, unlike legacy other.contacts[0] which allocated an array on the garbage collection heap on every frame!
notes: Collisions: What Did We Hit (7 min): Walk through OnCollisionEnter2D. Explain contact normals: normal.y > 0.5f means stomp! Demonstrate with simulator buttons.

title: Grabbing the Hit Object
content:
Grabbing the Hit GameObject

other parameter contains collision metadata (contacts, normal, impact force). To interact with the physical entity in the scene, access its GameObject: 

void OnCollisionEnter2D(Collision2D other) {
    // other.gameObject is the living object in scene
    GameObject hitObject = other.gameObject;
    Debug.Log($"Bumped into: {hitObject.name}");
}
Collision2D vs GameObject: Collision2D is a temporary C# data struct reporting where the hit occurred. other.gameObject is the actual object sitting in your Scene Hierarchy.
Common Trap: Collider vs GameObject
  • other.gameObject → The whole GameObject in Hierarchy.
  • other.collider → The specific Collider2D component hit.
  • other.transform → The position and rotation.
If an enemy has multiple child colliders (e.g. body collider + head trigger), other.collider points to the child, but other.gameObject gives you the root enemy entity!
[OBJECT COMMUNICATION ARCHITECTURE]
Player
BUMPS →
other.gameObject
Scene Hierarchy & Component Stack:
[GameObject: Goomba] → other.gameObject
  └ [Transform]
  └ [CircleCollider2D] → other.collider
  └ [Rigidbody2D]
  └ [Enemy.cs] → Target script to grab!
other.gameObject gives you the key to read any component on the touched enemy using TryGetComponent!
[Advanced] Multi-Collider Child Hierarchies Expand ▼
When colliders reside on child GameObjects, other.gameObject.GetComponentInParent<Enemy>() traverses up the transform hierarchy to find the master enemy script safely.
notes: other.gameObject (5 min): We have the collided GameObject reference. Ask class: 'Do we know if it's an enemy or a wall yet?' Transition into TryGetComponent.

title: TryGetComponent: The Safe Way to Check
content:
TryGetComponent: The Safe Way to Check

Legacy GetComponent() throws null crashes if the script is missing. TryGetComponent checks safely in 1 step: 

void OnCollisionEnter2D(Collision2D other) {
    if (other.gameObject.TryGetComponent(out Enemy enemy)) {
        enemy.TakeDamage(10); // Guaranteed safe!
    } else {
        // Not an enemy (wall, coin, ground)
    }
}
The 'out' Keyword: out Enemy enemy creates the variable and assigns it in the same expression. If found, it returns true and assigns the pointer. If missing, it returns false and sets enemy = null without throwing a crash!
Why TryGetComponent Wins
0 CRASHES Never throws NullReferenceException.
1 LOOKUP Checks existence and grabs reference in single pass.
0 GC Zero garbage collection allocations in hot collision loops.
[LIVE COMPONENT SCANNER SIMULATOR]
Scanner
Click action below
Target
Click an action above to simulate TryGetComponent.
[Advanced] Performance in High-Frequency Loops Expand ▼
In bullet hell shooters or rapid particle collisions, TryGetComponent prevents thousands of heap allocations per second, eliminating micro-stutter frame drops on mobile devices!
notes: TryGetComponent (7 min): Highlight why TryGetComponent beats legacy GetComponent (0 bytes GC, safe null check). Test Goomba vs Wall in simulator.

title: Tags: Always Use CompareTag
content:
Tags: Always Use CompareTag

Never use == for tag checks:

// DO THIS (0 GC allocations, native C++ comparison):
if (other.gameObject.CompareTag("Enemy")) { ... }

// DONT DO THIS (Allocates heap string every frame!):
if (other.gameObject.tag == "Enemy") { ... }
Why .tag == Causes Lag: The .tag property calls into C++ code to instantiate a brand new C# string object on the Managed Heap. In 60 FPS gameplay with multiple collisions, this floods the Garbage Collector!
CompareTag Rules
TYPO SAFE Throws console warning if tag isn't declared in Tag Manager.
0 BYTES Zero memory garbage. Pure internal hash comparison.
[LIVE MEMORY BENCHMARK: TAG COMPARISON]
Tag: "Enemy"
Heap Garbage Allocation:
Click a button above to test memory allocation.
[Advanced] Tag Manager Declaration Expand ▼
Using an undeclared tag with CompareTag throws an immediate Unity exception, catching typos before you build! .tag == fails silently, leaving bugs undetected.
notes: CompareTag (7 min): The classic micro-stutter bug! Explain why .tag == allocates strings on heap. Show Project Settings setup and run profiler.

title: Finding Objects in Scene
content:
Direct References: Safe, Instant, Zero Cost
Goomba says:

"Do NOT search the whole scene looking for me! Connect me directly via [SerializeField] in the Inspector!" 

// DO THIS: Direct serialized reference (0ms lookup, rename safe)
[SerializeField] private Player player;

// DONT DO THIS: Expensive O(n) scene search, breaks on rename
void Start() {
    player = GameObject.Find("Player").GetComponent();
}
Why GameObject.Find Breaks Games: 1. If anyone renames "Player" to "Player_Character", code breaks silently. 2. It scans all 5,000 scene objects sequentially (O(n) search). 3. Prefabs saved in the Project folder cannot find scene objects with Find!
If You MUST Find an Object in Code

For global managers or singletons, use Unity 6's type-safe method once in Awake(): 

GameManager gm = FindFirstObjectByType();
FindFirstObjectByType<T>() searches by exact C# type instead of string names. Never call this inside Update()!
[LIVE BENCHMARK: Scene Search vs Direct Pointer]
Click a button above to run scene search benchmark.
[Advanced] Unity 6 FindFirstObjectByType Expand ▼
Unity 6 deprecated legacy FindObjectOfType() because its search order was non-deterministic. Always use FindFirstObjectByType<T>() or FindAnyObjectByType<T>() in modern code.
notes: GameObject.Find (6 min): Comic slide. Emphasize: 'Never use GameObject.Find()'. Renaming objects breaks games. Run search cost simulator to show CPU penalty.

title: 2. Collections
subtitle: Arrays, Lists, Dictionaries & ScriptableObjects in Memory
content:
Memory Architecture
Games manage hundreds of items, enemies, and coordinates. Choosing the right collection data structure guarantees 60+ FPS performance and clean code.
notes: Part 2: Data Containers (2 min): Transition slide. 60 FPS games require efficient memory storage. Intro lockers, backpacks, phonebooks, and brains.

title: Arrays: Fixed Lockers
content:
T[] Array: Fixed Metal Lockers

Fixed-size container with numbered slots starting at index 0:

// Inspector exposed array with fixed slots
[SerializeField] private Transform[] spawnPoints;

void Start() {
    // Instant O(1) access by slot number:
    Transform firstPoint = spawnPoints[0];
}
Memory Architecture: Arrays store items in a single contiguous block of memory. This allows instant O(1) access because the computer simply calculates: base_address + (index * item_size).
When to Use Arrays & Out-of-Bounds Error

Use arrays when the number of items NEVER changes during gameplay (e.g. 4 spawn points, 3 difficulty modes).

IndexOutOfRangeException: If an array has 3 slots, valid indices are 0, 1, 2. Trying to access spawnPoints[3] immediately crashes your script with an out-of-bounds error!
[LIVE SIMULATOR: Metal Locker Slot Access]
Click a slot button above to test memory bounds.
[Advanced] Cache Lines & Contiguous Memory Expand ▼
Because arrays sit in contiguous memory, modern CPU hardware prefetches neighboring elements into high-speed L1/L2 CPU cache lines, making sequential array loops ultra fast!
notes: Arrays (7 min): The Metal Lockers metaphor. Fixed size, instant O(1) speed, shows in Inspector. Test opening slot 0, 1, and out of range error.

title: Lists: The Magic Backpack
content:
List<T>: The Magic Backpack

Dynamic container that expands and shrinks as you add or remove items:

using System.Collections.Generic;

[SerializeField] private List activeEnemies = new();

void Spawn(Enemy e) => activeEnemies.Add(e);
void Despawn(Enemy e) => activeEnemies.Remove(e);
Required Namespace: Always include using System.Collections.Generic; at the top of your script. Lists give you .Add(), .Remove(), .Contains(), and .Count.
When to Use Lists & Capacity Doubling

Use Lists when objects are spawned, destroyed, or collected dynamically (e.g. inventory items, active enemies).

Capacity vs Count: Under the hood, a List wraps an internal array. When full, it allocates a new array of DOUBLE the capacity (4 → 8 → 16) and copies items over. If you know you will spawn 100 enemies, initialize with new List<Enemy>(100) to prevent re-allocations!
[LIVE SIMULATOR: Dynamic Inventory Backpack]
Backpack Contents: 3 items
Health Potion Iron Sword Magic Ring
[Advanced] List.Remove Performance Cost Expand ▼
Calling list.RemoveAt(0) forces all remaining elements to shift left by one slot (O(n) copy). If order doesn't matter, swap with the last element and remove from the end for instant O(1) removal!
notes: Lists (7 min): The Magic Backpack metaphor. Grows and shrinks with .Add() and .Remove(). Pre-size capacity tip. Test backpack simulator.

title: Dictionaries: The Phone Book
content:
Dictionary<TKey, TValue>: The Phone Book

Key-value pair container providing instant lookup by unique name instead of index:

using System.Collections.Generic;

private Dictionary itemDatabase = new();

void Start() {
    itemDatabase.Add("potion_hp", new ItemData("HP Potion", 50));
    
    // Instant 1-step O(1) lookup by key:
    if (itemDatabase.TryGetValue("potion_hp", out ItemData item)) {
        Debug.Log("Found: " + item.name);
    }
}
Instant Hash Math: A Dictionary computes a mathematical hash code from the key string, pointing directly to the memory bucket holding that item in 1 single step.
Safe Lookup: TryGetValue vs KeyNotFoundException

Directly accessing itemDatabase["missing_key"] throws a crash! Always use TryGetValue.

Inspector Limitation: Standard C# Dictionaries do NOT show up in the Unity Inspector by default. To edit them visually, use parallel Arrays or custom serializable dictionary plugins.
[LIVE BENCHMARK: 1-Step Hash vs 428-Item Loop]
Click a lookup button above to test search speed.
[Expert] Hash Collisions & Buckets Expand ▼
If two different keys produce the same hash code (hash collision), Unity's dictionary places them in a linked list bucket. Best practice: use simple strings, ints, or enum keys for clean hashing.
notes: Dictionaries (7 min): The Phone Book metaphor. Instant search by key string. Run interactive phonebook search: 1 step vs 500-item sequential loop!

title: ScriptableObjects: 50 Goombas, 1 Brain
content:
ScriptableObjects: 50 Goombas, 1 Brain

Store stats in a shared .asset file on disk instead of duplicating variables on 50 GameObjects: 

[CreateAssetMenu(menuName = "Stats/Enemy")]
public class EnemyStatsSO : ScriptableObject {
    public float moveSpeed = 3.5f;
    public int maxHealth = 20;
}
Shared Memory Architecture: When 50 Goombas instantiate, each holds an 8-byte pointer to the SAME ScriptableObject asset in RAM. Changing the speed value in the Inspector immediately changes all 50 Goombas live!
Designer Friendly
1 EDIT Change moveSpeed once → all 50 Goombas update.
PRESETS FastGoomba.asset, TankGoomba.asset, Boss.asset.
[LIVE SHARED MEMORY SIMULATOR]

[Advanced] Play Mode Persistence Gotcha Expand ▼
Values changed on ScriptableObjects during Play Mode in the Editor STAY CHANGED even after stopping Play Mode! In published builds, they reset to default.
notes: ScriptableObjects (8 min): 50 Goombas, 1 Brain. Show side-by-side screenshots. Tune speed slider live to show 3 Goombas updating in Play Mode.

title: Collections & Data: Comparison Matrix
content:
Quick Comparison: Which One Should You Use?
Data Type Metaphor Can Resize? In Inspector? Best For (When to Use)
Array (T[]) Metal Lockers No (Fixed slots) Yes Fixed spawn points, weapon slots, fixed levels.
List (List<T>) Expanding Backpack Yes (Add / Remove) Yes (+ / - buttons) Live enemies in level, inventory loot, bullets.
Dictionary Phone Book Yes (Key-Value) No (Needs code) Fast search by name (e.g. items["Potion"]).
ScriptableObject Shared Brain File Yes (.asset file) Yes (Drag & drop) Shared enemy stats, balancing values, game settings.
Cheat Sheet: Simple Decision Rules
NEVER CHANGES?
Use an Array. Simplest and fastest.
SPAWNS & DIES?
Use a List. Grow and shrink on the fly.
SEARCH BY NAME?
Use a Dictionary. Instant key lookup.
SHARED GAME DATA?
Use a ScriptableObject. 50 enemies, 1 file.
[Advanced] 1-Line Code Summary Expand ▼ 
Transform[] waypoints = new Transform[4];        // Array: 4 fixed slots
List enemies = new();                     // List: dynamic add / remove
Dictionary scores = new();          // Dictionary: lookup by name string
[SerializeField] private EnemyStatsSO stats;     // ScriptableObject: shared asset file
[Expert] Memory Tip Expand ▼
Arrays allocate memory once. Lists allocate and expand as needed. ScriptableObjects share memory on disk across all prefab instances.
notes: Collections Matrix (6 min): Summary synthesis slide. Walk through cheat sheet rules: Never changes? Array. Spawns/dies? List. Search by name? Dictionary. Shared stats? SO.

title: 3. Timers and Events
subtitle: Controlling Cadence & Decoupling Systems with Observer Patterns
content:
Timing & Observer Patterns
Spawning waves of enemies, weapon cooldowns, and broadcasting player death to UI, Audio, and Save systems without spaghetti couplings.
notes: Part 3: Timers & Events (2 min): Transition slide. Introduce time management and decoupled architecture.

title: Timers: The Stopwatch in Update
content:
Stopwatch Accumulator in Update()

The standard frame-rate independent stopwatch pattern:

[SerializeField] private float interval = 2.0f;
private float timer = 0f;

void Update() {
    timer += Time.deltaTime; // Add frame duration
    if (timer >= interval) {
        SpawnEnemy();
        timer = 0f; // Reset stopwatch
    }
}
Time.deltaTime: The fractional seconds it took Unity to render the previous frame (e.g. 0.0166s at 60 FPS). Accumulating deltaTime guarantees your stopwatch ticks at the exact same speed regardless of player frame rate.
Time.deltaTime vs unscaledDeltaTime

When pausing your game with Time.timeScale = 0;, Time.deltaTime drops to 0!

For pause menu animations, cooldown countdowns, or UI timers that must keep ticking while gameplay is frozen, use Time.unscaledDeltaTime.
[LIVE SIMULATOR: Update Stopwatch Accumulator]
Accumulator Time: 0.00s / 2.0s
Accumulator idle.
[Advanced] Countdown vs Accumulator Expand ▼
Instead of adding up to an interval, you can start at timer = interval and subtract timer -= Time.deltaTime down to 0. Both patterns produce identical frame-rate independent results!
notes: Timers in Update (7 min): Kitchen Stopwatch metaphor. Run stopwatch demo. Call out unscaledDeltaTime for pause menus!

title: Coroutines: Take a Nap, Wake Up Later
content:
Coroutines: Asynchronous Pauses

Pause a method without freezing Unity's main thread:

private IEnumerator SpawnRoutine() {
    while (true) {
        // Pauses THIS method, but game keeps running!
        yield return new WaitForSeconds(2.0f);
        SpawnEnemy();
    }
}

// Start with: StartCoroutine(SpawnRoutine());
Lifecycle Control: Coroutines return IEnumerator. Started via StartCoroutine(). If the parent GameObject is disabled (SetActive(false)), all its running coroutines DIE instantly!
When to Use Coroutines & Golden Rule
  • Multi-Step Sequences: Fade screen → wait 2s → load new level.
  • Temporary Buffs: Star power invincibility lasts 8s → expires.
  • Periodic Spawners: Spawn enemy waves at regular intervals.
Golden Rule: NEVER write a while (true) loop without a yield! A loop with no yield locks Unity's main thread and crashes the editor.
[LIVE SIMULATOR: yield return WaitForSeconds]
Spawned Enemies: 0
Coroutine idle.
[Advanced] Cache Your WaitForSeconds Expand ▼
Writing yield return new WaitForSeconds(2.0f); inside a loop creates garbage memory allocations every loop! Instead, cache it: private readonly WaitForSeconds waitTwoSec = new(2.0f); and yield that cached object.
notes: Coroutines (8 min): Take a nap, wake up later. Explain yield return. Warn about while loops without yield. Mention caching WaitForSeconds.

title: Timers: InvokeRepeating Method
content:
InvokeRepeating: Simple Repeating Timer

The quickest way to repeat a void function without writing a loop:

void Start() {
    // Starts after 1.0s, repeats every 2.0s:
    InvokeRepeating(nameof(SpawnEnemy), 1.0f, 2.0f);
}

void OnDisable() {
    // ALWAYS cancel repeating timers when object is disabled!
    CancelInvoke(nameof(SpawnEnemy));
}
Parameters: 1. Method name, 2. Initial delay in seconds, 3. Repeat interval in seconds. Always use nameof(SpawnEnemy) instead of strings like "SpawnEnemy" so renaming your function in Rider updates automatically!
Limitations & Cleanup Rule

1. Cannot pass parameters to the invoked function. 2. Must call CancelInvoke() in OnDisable()!

If an object is disabled without cancelling, Unity keeps trying to invoke the method via string reflection, creating ghost timers running on inactive objects.
Timer Pattern Best For Can Pass Args?
Update Stopwatch Tight gameplay counters Yes
Coroutine Multi-step animations Yes
InvokeRepeating Quick prototype loops No
[Advanced] String Reflection Overhead Expand ▼
InvokeRepeating uses reflection under the hood to find the method by name string. Coroutines and Update timers are significantly faster in performance-critical production systems.
notes: InvokeRepeating (5 min): Quick alarm clock. Fast for game jams, but avoids parameters. Explain CancelInvoke() in OnDisable().

title: Events: Connecting Without Code
content:
UnityEvent: Inspector Drag & Drop Wiring

Let game designers hook up audio, particles, and UI without writing code:

using UnityEngine.Events;

public class Goomba : MonoBehaviour {
    [SerializeField] private UnityEvent onStomped;

    void Squash() {
        // Fire all wired actions in Inspector!
        onStomped?.Invoke();
    }
}
Inspector Workflow: Declaring [SerializeField] private UnityEvent onStomped; creates a clickable + list in the Inspector. Drag in any GameObject and pick any public function from the dropdown!
Decoupling: Goomba Knows Nothing!

Goomba doesn't know ScoreManager, SoundPlayer, or ParticleSystem exist!

Clean Architecture: If you delete the ScoreManager from the scene, Goomba won't crash with a NullReferenceException. The UnityEvent simply invokes whatever listeners are hooked up.
[LIVE SIMULATOR: UnityEvent Wiring]
Score Listener: 0 PTS
Click button to simulate UnityEvent execution.
[Advanced] UnityEvent Performance Profile Expand ▼
UnityEvents are serialized and invoke listeners through reflection. For ultra high-frequency combat events (e.g. 100 bullets hitting per frame), use C# Actions instead!
notes: UnityEvent (7 min): Lego bricks for designers. Zero code glue. Run Invoke simulator to show score updating.

title: C# Actions: Pure High-Speed Radio Broadcast
content:
C# Actions: High-Speed Radio Broadcast

Pure C# publisher/subscriber events with zero Inspector overhead:

// Publisher (Goomba.cs):
public static event System.Action onGoombaDied;
void Die() {
    onGoombaDied?.Invoke(); // Broadcasts to everyone!
}

// Subscriber (ScoreManager.cs):
void OnEnable() { Goomba.onGoombaDied += AddScore; }
void OnDisable() { Goomba.onGoombaDied -= AddScore; }
Always Unsubscribe: If you subscribe in OnEnable, always unsubscribe in OnDisable with -=. Forgetting creates memory leaks because the event holds the dead object in RAM!
Why C# Actions Win in Code
FAST 10x faster than UnityEvents in hot gameplay loops.
DECOUPLED Goomba has 0 references to Score, Audio, or UI.
[RADIO BROADCAST ARCHITECTURE SIMULATOR]
Tower: onDied
SoundManager → PlaySquish()
ScoreHUD → AddScore(100)
ParticleFX → SpawnStars()
Click above: Goomba shouts once → all 3 systems respond without Goomba knowing they exist!
[Advanced] Static vs Instance Events Expand ▼
Using static event Action allows any subscriber anywhere in the scene to listen without finding the Goomba instance! Perfect for global gameplay events like game over or score.
notes: C# Actions (7 min): Radio station pattern. High-frequency 60 FPS performance. Emphasize MANDATORY -= unsubscribe in OnDisable() to prevent memory leaks!

title: Events & Actions: Comparison Matrix
content:
UnityEvent vs C# System.Action
Feature UnityEvent C# System.Action
Primary Audience Game Designers & Level Builders Programmers & Core Systems
Setup Method Drag & Drop in Unity Inspector (0 code) C# Code Subscriptions (+= and -=)
Execution Speed Slower (Uses internal reflection & memory) Instant (Direct function pointer)
Unsubscribing Automatic (Handled by Unity) MANDATORY in OnDisable()!
Best Use Case Audio sound effects, particles, UI buttons 60 FPS physics loops, damage pipelines, game states
Decision Cheat Sheet
DESIGNER NEEDS CONTROL?
Use UnityEvent so audio and VFX hook up without code.
HIGH FREQUENCY (60 FPS)?
Use C# Action for maximum performance and zero garbage.
CROSS-SCENE BROADCAST?
Use a ScriptableObject GameEvent to decouple scenes.
[Advanced] Why C# Actions Leak Memory Expand ▼
If object A subscribes to object B with +=, object B holds a strong pointer to A. Even if A is destroyed, garbage collection cannot clean it up! Always unsubscribe with -= in OnDisable().
[Expert] Custom UnityEvent Listeners Expand ▼
In Unity 6, UnityEvent.AddListener is optimized, but delegate invocation in pure C# remains 10x faster in micro-benchmarks.
notes: Events Matrix (6 min): Decision table between UnityEvent and C# Action. Walk through cheat sheet: Designer? UnityEvent. 60 FPS? Action. Cross-scene? SO Event.

title: Practice Challenge 3: Spawner Loop & Death Event
notes: Give students 5 minutes. Goal is connecting the pieces: write a simple 2-second spawner coroutine, and fire a UnityEvent when an enemy dies so ScoreManager adds points without spaghetti coupling.
content:
[5-MIN CHALLENGE] Timers & Clean Events

Goal: Spawn enemies on a 2-second interval, and shout an event when an enemy dies!

  • Step 1 (Spawner): Write a Coroutine SpawnRoutine() that repeats: wait 2 seconds → spawn Goomba.
  • Step 2 (Event): Add [SerializeField] private UnityEvent onDied; on Goomba. When stomped, call onDied?.Invoke();.
  • Step 3 (Wiring): In the Inspector, click + on Goomba's event and wire it to ScoreManager.AddScore()!
// Scaffold:
private IEnumerator SpawnRoutine() {
    while (true) {
        yield return new WaitForSeconds(2.0f);
        Instantiate(goombaPrefab, transform.position, Quaternion.identity);
    }
}
Quick Decision Rule: What to Use When
TIMER Custom delays without Update mess? → Coroutine.
EVENT Hook up sound/UI in Inspector with 0 code? → UnityEvent.
FAST 100 bullets hitting per second? → System.Action.

title: Production Best Practices Checklist
content:
Production Best Practices Checklist
  • Transform Scale: Keep GameObject root scale at (1, 1, 1). Never stretch parent transform!
  • Pixels Per Unit (PPU): Keep PPU consistent across all sprites (e.g. 16 or 32).
  • Sprite Atlas: Combine small textures into single atlas to reduce draw calls.
  • Camera Framing: Set Orthographic Size properly to avoid sub-pixel jitter.
Why Scale (1,1,1) Matters: Scaling parent transforms distorts child 2D colliders, breaks Physics2D circle collision accuracy, and causes sprite tearing when rotating.
Mobile Optimization Golden Rules
DRAW CALLS Under 50 draw calls for mobile 60 FPS.
0 GC SPIKES Cache WaitForSeconds and use CompareTag.
[VISUAL BEST PRACTICES GUIDE]
[OK] Scale (1, 1, 1)
True circular physics collider
[BAD] Scale (2.2, 0.5, 1.0)
Squished deformed collider matrix
Sprite Atlas = 1 Single Draw Call
Instead of 30 separate texture draws, Atlas batches all character sprites into one GPU upload.
[Advanced] PhysX Matrix Deformation Expand ▼
Non-uniform scaling on parent transforms forces Box2D / PhysX to calculate skewed transformation matrices, doubling collision overhead.
notes: Production Checklist (6 min): Scale (1,1,1) physics warping diagram. Explain tunneling. Show visual child separation and [ContextMenu].

title: 5. Mobile Publishing: Google Play & itch.io
content:
1. Google Play Store (Commercial Path)
AAB Build Android App Bundle (.aab), not standalone APK!
KEY Generate and back up your Keystore signature file.
API 34+ Set Target API Level to Android 14 (API 34) or higher.
20 TESTERS Personal accounts need 14 continuous days with 20 testers.
Commercial Checklist: Requires $25 one-time developer registration fee. In Player Settings → Other Settings, set Scripting Backend to IL2CPP and enable ARM64 architecture.
2. itch.io Mobile (Student & Game Jam Path)

Fastest way to distribute your game for course grading and peer playtesting:

  • Build Direct APK: In Build Settings, leave Build App Bundle unchecked → export .apk.
  • Upload to itch.io: In project dashboard, upload .apk → check Android icon.
  • Instant Distribution: Classmates download APK, tap Install, and play in 30 seconds!
Why itch.io for Students: 100% Free ($0), zero review delay (publishes in 1 second), and NO 20-tester closed beta gatekeeping! Players just enable Install Unknown Apps in Android Settings.

[Advanced] Android Sideloading Permissions Expand ▼
When installing an APK downloaded from itch.io, Android displays a prompt: For your security, your phone is not allowed to install unknown apps from this source. Tap Settings → Allow from this source → tap Install.

You can also build for WebGL with touch controls and host directly on itch.io! Players can run your game directly inside their mobile phone browser with 0 installation required.
notes: Explain both paths clearly to students. Google Play is the commercial path ($25 fee, 20 testers for 14 days, AAB). itch.io is the essential student path (free, instant APK download, perfect for course hand-ins and rapid peer playtesting).

title: Capstone Challenge: End-to-End Spawner System
content:
Starter Package & Scene Setup

Download the official starter package and import it into your Unity project:

Download basics2.unitypackage (Direct) View on GitHub Repo [link]
Import Instructions: In Unity top menu → Assets > Import Package > Custom Package → select basics2.unitypackage → click Import All. Open scene: Assets/Scenes/0_startscene.unity.
Capstone Challenge: 4 Integration Milestones
  1. Milestone 1 (Spawn Points Array): In EnemySpawner.cs, create [SerializeField] private Transform[] spawnPoints;. In Inspector, assign your 3 scene spawn points.
  2. Milestone 2 (Shared Brain SO): Create EnemyStatsSO (speed: 3.5, hp: 20). Assign this asset to your Goomba prefab so all spawned enemies share 1 brain.
  3. Milestone 3 (Wave Coroutine): Write an IEnumerator SpawnRoutine() that loops: wait 2.0s → pick random spawn point → instantiate Goomba → add to List<Enemy> activeEnemies.
  4. Milestone 4 (Decoupled Death Event): When Goomba is stomped, fire onDied?.Invoke() → removes itself from Spawner's List, adds 100 points to ScoreManager, and squashes!
Architecture Check: Notice how Goomba does NOT have a hard-coded reference to ScoreManager or the Spawner. Everything communicates cleanly through events and parameters. Zero spaghetti code!
[SUCCESS CRITERIA & ARCHITECTURE CHECKLIST]
  • [OK] Array used for fixed spawn points (size never changes).
  • [OK] List used for living enemies (expands/shrinks dynamically).
  • [OK] ScriptableObject stores stats once (no duplicated numbers).
  • [OK] Coroutine controls 2.0s timing without Update timer mess.
  • [OK] OnCollisionEnter2D checks normal.y > 0.5f for stomp.
  • [OK] UnityEvent / Action broadcasts death (zero coupling).
  • [OK] Zero Console errors or unhandled null references!
Ready for Next Milestone!
Completing this challenge means your game has a robust, production-grade architecture ready for full level design and mobile publishing.
[Advanced] Object Pooling with UnityEngine.Pool Expand ▼
Instead of calling Instantiate() and Destroy() repeatedly (which triggers garbage collection spikes on mobile CPUs), recycle Goombas using Unity 6's built-in UnityEngine.Pool.ObjectPool<GameObject>!
[Expert] Finite State Machine (Patrol & Squash) Expand ▼
Structure Goomba AI using a clean enum State Machine: 
public enum GoombaState { Patrol, Alert, Squashed }
public void ChangeState(GoombaState newState) { ... }
notes: This is the final hands-on workshop combining all concepts: Arrays for spawn points, Lists for tracking active enemies, ScriptableObjects for shared stats, Coroutines for wave delays, and Events for death notifications. Ensure all students download basics2.unitypackage and open 0_startscene.unity.
